ta-l1d31q1-d1e100.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 31. Having treated what is proper to the persons, Lombard turns to what is appropriated to them, and then (Dist. 32) to how the persons compare with one another by these appropriations. He first explains the meaning of names appropriated to the persons: 'equality', then 'like' and 'likeness', approving the view that such names remove rather than posit something. He then sets out the saints' appropriations: Hilary's (eternity in the Father, species in the Image, use in the Gift), with Augustine's exposition and Lombard's removal of doubts about it, and Augustine's own (unity in the Father, equality in the Son, connection in the Holy Spirit), with the reasons for each and a note on how 'one' is said in the neuter and masculine. Thomas announces four topics: equality; appropriation in general; the reason for Hilary's appropriation; and Augustine's appropriation.
claims: Appropriated names are distinguished from proper names.
Hilary and Augustine each give a triad of appropriations.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e146.summary: Presupposing Dist. 19, the article asks whether equality posits anything in God, with a first argument that it does. Whatever is in God and creatures is nobler in God, and equality and likeness posit something in creatures.
claims: What is in creatures is nobler in God.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e149.summary: Second argument. Arius was condemned for denying the equality of the persons, and he would not have been a heretic unless he denied something in God.
claims: Denying equality was heresy.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e152.summary: Third argument. Equality seems to be the one essence undifferentiated in three persons, as the text says, and that essence is something positive in God.
claims: Equality is the one undifferentiated essence.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e156.summary: Fourth argument. Equality is a relation, and relation predicates something positive, not privative.
claims: Relation is positive.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e159.summary: Sed contra from Lombard in the text.
claims: Equality posits nothing in God.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e162.summary: Second sed contra. The Philosopher says the equal is opposed to the great and small as a double privation and is defined privatively, and privation predicates nothing positive.
claims: The equal is defined privatively.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e165.summary: Thomas's determination. Equality is a relation founded on unity of quantity, in God on unity of essence signified as virtual quantity (magnitude, eternity, power). It can be considered as to the unity of quantity that causes it, and then its character consists in privation, like unity (Dist. 24), so the equal is opposed privatively to great and small as one to many; or as to the consequent relation, and then in creatures it posits something really in both extremes, but in the divine persons only conceptually. If it posited a real relation in the persons, this would come either from the essence, which is numerically one, and the same is not really related to itself (Dist. 26), or from the persons constituted by relations, and a relation is not related by a further real relation, or there would be an infinite regress. So, with Lombard, equality said of God posits only a relation of name or reason, though it does posit unity of essence, not as part of its concept but as presupposed, as with privatives and names said from time.
claims: Equality in God is a relation of reason founded on the unity of essence.
As to its foundation, equality consists in privation, like unity.
A real relation of equality in God would require relating the essence to itself or relations to relations.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e168.summary: Reply to the first argument. As to unity taken universally, as convertible with being, equality posits nothing positive in God or creatures, any more than unity does. But in creatures the supposits of equality are absolute, so they are related by a mediating real relation, which does not hold in God.
claims: In creatures absolute supposits need a real mediating relation; in God not.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e171.summary: Reply to the second argument. Although equality is conceptual, the relation has something corresponding in reality, which is why denying equality is heresy, as denying that God is Lord would be, though that relation posits nothing in God.
claims: A relation of reason with a real foundation can be denied heretically.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e175.summary: Reply to the third argument. As in creatures equality is not the one quantity of several but a relation including such unity, in God equality is not the one essence but a conceptual relation following the unity of essence.
claims: Equality is a relation following unity of essence, not the essence itself.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e178.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. That relation cannot be really in God, so being said relatively does not make it posit something.
claims: Being relative does not entail real positing.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e190.summary: First argument that essential attributes should not be appropriated to the persons. What is common to several should be appropriated to none, and all attributes are common to the three.
claims: The common should not be appropriated.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e193.summary: Second argument. Like things are judged alike, and all attributes signify the common essence, so either all or none should be appropriated, and all to one person.
claims: All attributes are alike in signifying the essence.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e196.summary: Third argument. The appropriated conceptually follows the proper, since the proper falls in its concept, but essential attributes can be understood without the propers, as unbelievers do.
claims: Attributes are understood without the propers.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e200.summary: Fourth argument. We should do nothing that may lead to error in faith, and appropriating something common to one person may lead people to think it belongs only or more to that person.
claims: Appropriation risks error.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e203.summary: Sed contra from the authority of Hilary and Augustine in the text.
claims: The saints appropriate.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e206.summary: Second sed contra. The processions are distinguished and named by different attribute concepts, the Spirit proceeding by way of will and the Son by way of nature, so an attribute fitting a person's procession can be appropriated to that person.
claims: Processions are named from attributes.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e209.summary: Thomas's determination. Appropriation is fitting both on the side of the thing and on our side. Though the essential attributes are common to the three, one attribute by its concept is more like the proper of one person than of another and so can fittingly be appropriated to that person: power, which includes the character of principle, to the Father, principle not from a principle; wisdom to the Son, who proceeds as Word; goodness to the Spirit, who proceeds as love, whose object is the good. This likeness of the appropriated to the proper makes appropriation fitting on the side of the thing, which would hold even if we did not exist. On our side, its usefulness makes it fitting: there is distinction and order both in the attributes, conceptually, and in the persons, really, so though the attributes do not suffice to reach the propers of the persons, we see in the appropriated some likeness of the persons, so appropriation helps manifest the faith, imperfectly, as do vestige and image.
claims: An attribute is appropriated to a person when its concept resembles that person's proper.
Power is appropriated to the Father, wisdom to the Son, goodness to the Spirit.
Appropriation manifests the faith imperfectly, like vestige and image.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e212.summary: Reply to the first argument. That an attribute belongs to all proves it is not proper to one person but not that it is not appropriated, since the prefix 'ad' signifies approach with some distance: as Augustine says, man, imitating God with a distance of likeness, is image and 'to the image', while the Son, imitating the Father without unlikeness, is image and not 'to the image'. Attributes approach the propers by likeness and are distant by commonness, so they are rightly called appropriated.
claims: 'Ad-propriare' means approaching the proper with a distance.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e215.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though the attributes are really one, they differ conceptually and by their concepts resemble the origin of persons (power as principle of production) or a determinate mode of origin (goodness the procession of love, wisdom that of the Word), so they can be appropriated to different persons. 'Essence' by its concept says neither origin nor anything about its mode, so it is not appropriated.
claims: Attributes resembling origin or its modes are appropriated; 'essence' is not.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e219.summary: Reply to the third argument. 'Appropriated' can be taken materially, for what is appropriated, and so the attribute does not follow the concept of the proper; or formally, as appropriated, and so it includes the concept of the proper.
claims: Formally, the appropriated includes reference to the proper.

ta-l1d31q1-d1e222.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Appropriating essential attributes to persons does not exclude the other persons or set up degrees of participation; it only shows the likeness of the appropriated concept to the person's proper, so no error follows.
claims: Appropriation excludes no person and sets no degree.

ta-l1d31q1-Dd1e92.summary: The opening section of Distinction 31 divides Lombard's treatment of appropriations, explaining 'equality' and 'likeness' and setting out Hilary's and Augustine's triads, and announces four topics: equality, appropriation in general, Hilary's appropriation, and Augustine's.
claims: Appropriated names follow proper names.

ta-l1d31q1-Dd1e138.summary: Article 1 holds that equality in God is only a relation of reason founded on the unity of essence. As to its foundation it consists in privation, like unity, and a real relation of equality would require the essence to be related to itself or relations to relations. It presupposes unity of essence, and denying it is heresy because it has a real foundation.
claims: Equality in God is a relation of reason founded on unity of essence.

ta-l1d31q1-Dd1e182.summary: Article 2 holds that essential attributes are fittingly appropriated to persons when their concept resembles a person's proper: power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, goodness to the Spirit. This holds on the side of the thing and is useful to us as an imperfect manifestation of the faith. Appropriation approaches the proper with distance, 'essence' is not appropriated, and appropriation excludes no person.
claims: Attributes are appropriated by likeness to the persons' propers.
Appropriation manifests the faith without excluding any person.

ta-l1d31q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 31 treats equality and appropriation in general. Article 1 holds that equality in God is a relation of reason founded on the unity of essence, privative as to its foundation. Article 2 holds that essential attributes are appropriated to the persons by the likeness of their concepts to the persons' propers, power to the Father, wisdom to the Son, and goodness to the Spirit, which is fitting in reality and useful as an imperfect manifestation of the Trinity.
claims: Equality in God is a relation of reason founded on unity of essence.
Attributes are appropriated to persons by likeness to their propers.
